image_query: Madhubani Mithila folk painting wall mural
tweets: In 1934 a massive earthquake tore through Bihar — and when officials inspected the cracked mud homes, they found something no outsider had ever recorded: walls painted edge to edge in dazzling patterns, by women whose names no history book had bothered to ask.

This was Madhubani (Mithila) painting — passed mother to daughter for generations in Bihar's villages. Women freshly plastered their walls with mud and cow dung, then painted them for weddings and festivals using twigs, matchsticks, and even fingertips as brushes.

The style follows one rule: leave no space empty. Every gap fills with fish, peacocks, lotuses, and geometric borders — each motif symbolic of fertility, prosperity, or protection. Pigments are entirely natural: turmeric yellow, indigo blue, rice-paste white, soot black.

It was British officer W.G. Archer who first photographed these wall paintings after the 1934 quake and published them in 1949. In the 1960s, drought-relief workers encouraged artists to paint on paper instead of walls — and Madhubani art reached the world.

Artists like Sita Devi and Ganga Devi later won Padma Shri honors, and in 2007 Madhubani painting earned a GI tag protecting its name. Walls that once held a village's stories now hang in museums worldwide.
